Kubernetes Services

Why Services exist, how one apply becomes a virtual IP, a list of Pods, rules on every node and a DNS name — then every field, type, command and CKAD task, on the Jahez EKS cluster in me-central-1.

v3 · Part I High Level · Part II Low Level · Part III Practices & labs
Part I · High Level

1. Foundations

1.1Introduction

In one sentenceA Service gives a changing group of Pods one stable name, one stable virtual IP and port, and spreads new connections across the Ready ones.

A Service is a built-in Kubernetes API object (apiVersion: v1, kind: Service), part of every cluster since v1.0. You do not install anything to use it: four built-in parts work together — the API server stores it and allocates its IP, the EndpointSlice controller (in kube-controller-manager) lists its Pods, kube-proxy on every node programs the packet rules, and CoreDNS answers its name. On Jahez EKS in me-central-1, kube-proxy and CoreDNS are EKS add-ons, Pod IPs come from the VPC CNI, and LoadBalancer Services are built by the AWS Load Balancer Controller.

✓ It is

  • a stable front door — one name, one virtual IP and one port — for a group of Pods that keeps changing
  • layer-4 load spreading: each new TCP/UDP connection goes to one Ready Pod
  • service discovery: CoreDNS turns the Service name into its IP
  • a way to expose Pods outside the cluster (NodePort, LoadBalancer)
  • a DNS alias for something outside the cluster (ExternalName)

✕ It is not

  • a process or a Pod — nothing "runs" as the Service; it is data plus rules on every node
  • an HTTP router — no paths, hosts or TLS termination (that is Ingress or Gateway API)
  • a health checker — it trusts the Pods' readiness probes
  • per-request balancing — one kept-alive connection stays on one Pod (gRPC / HTTP/2 trap)
  • a firewall — anyone who can route to it can call it (use NetworkPolicy)

Definitions

Pod IP
What it is
The private IP of one Pod. On Jahez EKS the VPC CNI gives each Pod a real VPC address from its node's subnet, e.g. 10.0.41.23 in me-central-1a.
🎯 Why it exists
Every Pod needs an address so packets can reach it — but the address belongs to that Pod only.
📄 What it looks like
YAMLpod-ip.yaml
status:
  podIP: 10.0.41.23
  hostIP: 10.0.41.17   # the node
⚙ What Kubernetes does
The CNI plugin assigns it when the Pod starts and releases it when the Pod dies. A replacement Pod gets a new IP.
Beforeorder-api-…-x2kqp = 10.0.41.23
→
AfterPod replaced → order-api-…-p9d2s = 10.0.41.57
📍 Where it lives
Pod status.podIP, written by the kubelet. Unique in the whole cluster.
⚠ Watch out
Never put a Pod IP in config. It is the problem Services solve (see §1.2).
Service
What it is
A core/v1 API object that names a group of Pods and gives them one stable virtual IP and DNS name.
🎯 Why it exists
Callers need an address that survives Pod restarts, scaling and deploys.
📄 What it looks like
YAMLservice.yaml
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: order-api-service
spec:
  selector:
    app: order-api
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: http
⚙ What Kubernetes does
The API server stores it and allocates a ClusterIP; controllers and kube-proxy build the rest (§2.3).
Beforecallers use 3 Pod IPs
→
Aftercallers use order-api-service:80
📍 Where it lives
etcd, in namespace jahez-prod. Namespaced.
⚠ Watch out
kubectl create service sets selector: app=<service name> — it usually matches nothing (§7.2).
Label selector
What it is
The key=value filter in spec.selector. Every Pod whose labels contain all these pairs is a backend.
🎯 Why it exists
The Service must find its Pods without anyone listing IPs.
📄 What it looks like
YAMLlabel-selector.yaml
spec:
  selector:
    app: order-api      # Pods need this exact label
⚙ What Kubernetes does
The EndpointSlice controller watches Pods and keeps every match that is Ready.
Beforeselector app: order-api, Pod label app: orders
→
After0 backends — no error anywhere, calls just fail
📍 Where it lives
Service spec.selector + Pod metadata.labels (from the Deployment template).
⚠ Watch out
A typo gives an empty Service silently. Check kubectl get endpointslices first (§7.6).
ClusterIP
What it is
The Service's virtual IP from the Service range (172.20.0.0/16 on Jahez EKS). No network card has it — only rules on every node.
🎯 Why it exists
A fixed address that never changes while the Service exists.
📄 What it looks like
YAMLclusterip.yaml
spec:
  clusterIP: 172.20.75.246   # chosen by the API server
⚙ What Kubernetes does
The API server allocates it once; kube-proxy on every node rewrites packets sent to it towards one Pod.
BeforeService created, no IP
→
After172.20.75.246 forever (until deleted)
📍 Where it lives
spec.clusterIP + a ServiceCIDR/IPAddress object in the API server.
⚠ Watch out
It is immutable: changing it gives may not change once set. ping to it does not answer — it only handles the Service ports.
Ports: port · targetPort · nodePort
What it is
port = what callers dial on the ClusterIP; targetPort = where the Pod listens (number or the container port's name); nodePort = a port opened on every node.
🎯 Why it exists
Callers and Pods may use different ports, and outside callers need a port on the nodes.
📄 What it looks like
YAMLports:-port-·-targetport-·-nodeport.yaml
ports:
  - name: http
    port: 80          # order-api-service:80
    targetPort: http  # container port "http" = 8080
    nodePort: 30080   # only NodePort / LoadBalancer
⚙ What Kubernetes does
kube-proxy rewrites ClusterIP:port → PodIP:targetPort.
Before172.20.75.246:80
→
After10.0.41.23:8080
📍 Where it lives
spec.ports[] of the Service; containerPort lives in the Pod.
⚠ Watch out
With 2+ ports every port needs a name. A wrong targetPort is accepted and fails only at call time.
EndpointSlice
What it is
An object that lists the Pod IPs and ports behind one Service, with their state (ready, serving, terminating) and zone.
🎯 Why it exists
kube-proxy and CoreDNS need the current backend list; slices hold up to 100 endpoints each so updates stay small.
📄 What it looks like
YAMLendpointslice.yaml
kind: EndpointSlice
metadata:
  labels:
    kubernetes.io/service-name: order-api-service
endpoints:
  - addresses: ["10.0.41.23"]
    conditions:
      ready: true
⚙ What Kubernetes does
The EndpointSlice controller rewrites it every time a matching Pod starts, becomes Ready, or goes away.
Before3 Ready Pods
→
Afterslice order-api-service-7xk2p lists 3 IPs
📍 Where it lives
etcd, same namespace, linked by the label kubernetes.io/service-name.
⚠ Watch out
The old Endpoints object is deprecated since v1.33 — read slices instead (§4.4).
kube-proxy
What it is
A DaemonSet (one Pod per node) that turns Services and EndpointSlices into kernel packet rules: iptables, IPVS or nftables.
🎯 Why it exists
The virtual IP must work on every node, for every Pod, with no extra hop.
📄 What it looks like
CMDshell
-A KUBE-SERVICES -d 172.20.75.246/32 -p tcp --dport 80 -j KUBE-SVC-HMBXK3VY6A3W2RQM
⚙ What Kubernetes does
Watches the API server and rewrites rules within a second of a change.
Beforepacket to 172.20.75.246:80
→
Afterpacket to 10.0.41.23:8080
📍 Where it lives
kube-system namespace; on EKS it is the kube-proxy add-on.
⚠ Watch out
If kube-proxy is down on a node, that node keeps old rules — calls go to dead Pods (§6.0).
Service DNS name
What it is
The name CoreDNS answers for every Service: <service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local.
🎯 Why it exists
Code should use names, not IPs.
📄 What it looks like
CMDshell
# inside any jahez-prod Pod
order-api-service                              # short form
order-api-service.jahez-prod.svc.cluster.local # full name (FQDN)
⚙ What Kubernetes does
CoreDNS watches Services and answers an A record with the ClusterIP (or the Pod IPs for headless).
Beforeorder-api-service
→
After172.20.75.246
📍 Where it lives
CoreDNS in kube-system, at 172.20.0.10; each Pod's /etc/resolv.conf points there.
⚠ Watch out
Short names only work inside the same namespace; ndots:5 makes external names slow (§5.3).
Service type
What it is
The field spec.type that decides who can reach the Service: ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer or ExternalName (headless = ClusterIP with clusterIP: None).
🎯 Why it exists
Inside callers, ops on a node, the internet and outside databases need different doors.
📄 What it looks like
YAMLservice-type.yaml
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer   # also creates the NodePort + ClusterIP parts
⚙ What Kubernetes does
Each type adds parts: ClusterIP → + port on every node → + cloud load balancer.
Beforetype: ClusterIP
→
Aftertype: LoadBalancer → AWS NLB hostname
📍 Where it lives
spec.type. Default ClusterIP.
⚠ Watch out
LoadBalancer creates one AWS NLB per Service — cost adds up; share via Ingress/Gateway (§1.4).
Readiness
What it is
A Pod condition from its readinessProbe. Only Ready Pods get Service traffic.
🎯 Why it exists
A Pod that is starting or overloaded should be skipped without being killed.
📄 What it looks like
YAMLreadiness.yaml
readinessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /health/ready
    port: http
  periodSeconds: 5
⚙ What Kubernetes does
The EndpointSlice controller sets conditions.ready from it; kube-proxy only sends to ready endpoints.
BeforePod warming its cache → ready: false
→
Afterremoved from rules until ready: true
📍 Where it lives
Pod spec.containers[].readinessProbe; result in status.conditions.
⚠ Watch out
No probe = Ready as soon as the container starts — traffic arrives before the app listens.

1.2Problems or needs

In one sentenceWithout Services, callers must chase changing Pod IPs by hand, balance load themselves, ignore readiness, and have no door from outside.

Life before Services, step by step, on the Jahez order flow. Each step shows what breaks and the manual commands you would need.

Step 1 / 5 · Only a Pod IP
Wheremenu-api → order-apiBlocksPod IPCommandkubectl get pods -o wide
  • menu-api must call order-api to show a customer's open orders.
  • There is no shared name, so you look up a Pod IP and hardcode it in menu-api's config.
Manual commands, in order
CMDwhat you would type
# 1. find the Pod IP
kubectl get pods -l app=order-api -n jahez-prod -o wide
# 2. hardcode it in the caller
kubectl set env deploy/menu-api-deployment ORDER_API_URL=http://10.0.41.23:8080 -n jahez-prod
OUTExample outputexample — needs running Pods
NAME                                    READY   STATUS    IP           NODE
order-api-deployment-7d9f8c6b5-x2kqp    1/1     Running   10.0.41.23   ip-10-0-41-17.me-central-1.compute.internal
What hurts
It works today — but the address belongs to one Pod.
← Prev1 / 5
Step 2 / 5 · Pod restarts → new IP
Wherenode-aBlocksPod IPCommandkubectl delete pod …
  • The Pod is replaced: an OOM kill, a node drain for an AMI update, or a new image.
  • The replacement gets 10.0.41.57. menu-api still calls 10.0.41.23 → connection refused, orders page fails at lunch peak.
Manual commands, in order
CMDwhat you would type
# the Pod is replaced (here by hand, in real life by a drain or OOM)
kubectl delete pod order-api-deployment-7d9f8c6b5-x2kqp -n jahez-prod
# find the new IP
kubectl get pods -l app=order-api -n jahez-prod -o wide
# update every caller again
kubectl set env deploy/menu-api-deployment ORDER_API_URL=http://10.0.41.57:8080 -n jahez-prod
OUTExample outputexample — needs running Pods
HttpRequestException: Connection refused (10.0.41.23:8080)
What hurts
Every Pod restart becomes a config change in every caller.
2 / 5
Step 3 / 5 · 3 replicas — which one?
Where3 nodesBlocksPod IP × 3Commandkubectl scale …
  • Lunch traffic needs 3 replicas across me-central-1a/b/c.
  • menu-api knows one IP. To use all three, every caller (12 .NET services) needs the list and its own load-balancing code.
Manual commands, in order
CMDwhat you would type
kubectl scale deploy/order-api-deployment --replicas=3 -n jahez-prod
kubectl get pods -l app=order-api -n jahez-prod -o wide
# copy 3 IPs into 12 callers and write round-robin code in each
What hurts
One Pod is hot, two are idle, and the IP list is stale after every change.
3 / 5
Step 4 / 5 · Deploys & not-ready Pods
Whererolling updateBlocksReadinessCommandkubectl rollout restart …
  • During a rollout new Pods start (warming caches for ~20 s) while old ones terminate.
  • A hand-kept list cannot know which Pods are ready, so callers hit starting or stopping Pods → 502s.
Manual commands, in order
CMDwhat you would type
kubectl rollout restart deploy/order-api-deployment -n jahez-prod
kubectl get pods -l app=order-api -n jahez-prod -w   # watch Pods come and go
# edit the IP list again — by hand, mid-rollout
What hurts
Zero-downtime deploys are impossible without a live, readiness-aware list.
4 / 5
Step 5 / 5 · Different callers, different doors
Whereinside · node · internet · AWSBlockseverythingCommandcurl …
  • The customer app on the internet cannot route to private VPC Pod IPs.
  • An ops engineer wants to hit order-api through a node for a quick test.
  • order-api must reach Amazon RDS outside the cluster — its endpoint is pasted in config.
  • Each Postgres replica must find its peers by a fixed name, not by load-balanced IP.
Manual commands, in order
CMDwhat you would type
# from a laptop on the internet — times out
curl -m 5 http://10.0.41.23:8080/health
# the RDS endpoint is pasted into every service's settings
aws rds describe-db-instances --db-instance-identifier payments-db --query 'DBInstances[0].Endpoint.Address'
kubectl set env deploy/order-api-deployment PAYMENTS_DB_HOST=payments-db.c9akciq32.me-central-1.rds.amazonaws.com -n jahez-prod
OUTExample outputexample — needs running Pods
curl: (28) Connection timed out after 5001 milliseconds
What hurts
No standard way in, and no standard name for anything outside.
5 / 5Next →

How Kubernetes removes all five problems → 1.3 Solution

1.3Solution

In one sentenceOne Service object per group of Pods: a stable name and ClusterIP up front, a live list of Ready Pods behind, and rules on every node that connect the two.

The solution in six steps

  1. Label the Pods. The Deployment template already sets app: order-api on every Pod.
  2. Write one Service with selector: app: order-api and port: 80 → targetPort: http.
  3. Apply it. The API server gives it ClusterIP 172.20.75.246; CoreDNS answers order-api-service.jahez-prod.svc.cluster.local.
  4. The EndpointSlice controller lists the Ready Pods: 10.0.41.23 · 10.0.77.140 · 10.0.118.9.
  5. kube-proxy on every node writes rules: 172.20.75.246:80 → one of the 3 Pods :8080.
  6. Callers use the name: ORDER_API_URL=http://order-api-service — never an IP again.

The real folder tree

jahez-k8s/
└─ apps/
   ├─ order-api/
   │  ├─ order-api-deployment.yaml        # Pods labelled app: order-api
   │  └─ order-api-service.yaml           # ClusterIP  → in-cluster callers
   ├─ orders-db/
   │  ├─ orders-db-stateful-set.yaml      # Postgres replicas
   │  └─ orders-db-headless-service.yaml  # Headless   → per-Pod DNS names
   ├─ storefront-gateway/
   │  ├─ storefront-gateway-deployment.yaml
   │  └─ storefront-gateway-service.yaml  # LoadBalancer → AWS NLB, internet
   ├─ ops-debug/
   │  └─ order-api-node-port-service.yaml # NodePort   → <node-ip>:30080
   ├─ payments-db/
   │  └─ payments-db-service.yaml         # ExternalName → Amazon RDS
   └─ loyalty-legacy/
      ├─ loyalty-api-service.yaml         # no selector …
      └─ loyalty-api-endpoint-slice.yaml  # … backends listed by hand

How each problem from 1.2 disappears

Problem from 1.2How the Service removes itWhere to read more
① Only a Pod IPCallers use the name order-api-service; CoreDNS answers the ClusterIP.§5.0
② Pod restarts → new IPThe ClusterIP never changes; the EndpointSlice controller swaps the Pod IP in the list within a second.§4.0
③ 3 replicas — which one?kube-proxy spreads new connections across all Ready Pods on every node.§6.0
④ Deploys & not-ready PodsOnly ready: true endpoints get traffic; terminating Pods drain.§4.1
⑤ Different doorsOne spec.type per caller: ClusterIP, Headless, NodePort, LoadBalancer, ExternalName.§3.3

1.4Comparisons

In one sentencePick the Service type by who must reach the Pods; pick Ingress or Gateway API when you need HTTP routing; pick the kube-proxy mode by cluster size.

The five Service types compared

ClusterIPHeadlessNodePortLoadBalancerExternalName
Gets a virtual IP?✓ 172.20.75.246✕ None✓✓✕
Reachable frominside the clusterinside the cluster+ anyone who can reach a node IP+ the internet / VPC via cloud LBwhatever the target allows
Address callers useorder-api-service:80orders-db-stateful-set-0.orders-db-headless-service<node-ip>:30080NLB hostname :443payments-db-service:5432
Also creates—per-Pod DNS recordsClusterIP partNodePort + ClusterIP parts (no NodePort when allocateLoadBalancerNodePorts: false)only a CNAME
Who picks the Podkube-proxythe client (DNS gives all IPs)kube-proxyAWS NLB → kube-proxy, or NLB → Pod (ip targets)no Pods involved
Uses selector?✓✓✓✓✕ ignored
Jahez useevery internal APIorders-db, Kafka, Redis clusterops debug onlystorefront-gateway (public)RDS, Amazon MSK, partner APIs
Main trapnot reachable from outsideno balancing, client must retryport range 30000-32767, every node opens itone NLB per Service = costno ports remapped, TLS names mismatch

Service vs Ingress vs Gateway API

ServiceIngressGateway API
LayerL4 — TCP / UDP / SCTPL7 — HTTP / HTTPSL4 + L7 (HTTPRoute, GRPCRoute, TLSRoute, TCPRoute)
Routes byIP + port onlyhost + pathhost, path, headers, method, weights
TLSpasses throughterminates at the controllerterminates or passes through, per listener
Built bykube-proxy + cloud controlleran Ingress controller (e.g. AWS LB Controller → ALB)a Gateway controller (AWS LB Controller, Envoy Gateway, Istio…)
Objects1 Service1 Ingress + Services behind itGatewayClass → Gateway → Routes → Services
Statuscore, stablestable, frozen — no new featuresGA (v1), the recommended successor to Ingress
Jahez useevery app (also behind Ingress/Gateway)existing ALB for jahez.net APIsnew public APIs, canary weights
When to choose something else
  • Many public HTTP APIs → one Gateway (or Ingress) with one load balancer in front of many ClusterIP Services, not one LoadBalancer Service each.
  • Per-request balancing for gRPC / HTTP/2 → a mesh (Istio, Linkerd) or client-side balancing over a headless Service.
  • Blocking who may call → NetworkPolicy; a Service never restricts callers.
  • Calling services in another cluster → multi-cluster Services (MCS API) or a mesh, not ExternalName.

kube-proxy modes compared

iptablesIPVSnftables
How it picks a Podrandom, per connection (statistic --probability)round-robin by default; also least-conn, source-hash…random, per connection (numgen map)
Cost per packetwalks rule lists — grows with Serviceshash lookup — flatmap lookup — flat
Rule updatesslow full rewrites at 10k+ Servicesfastfast, incremental
Status upstreamdefault on most clustersworks, but upstream steers new clusters to nftablesGA since v1.33
On Jahez EKS✓ current mode (EKS add-on default)possible via add-on configcheck the kube-proxy add-on version first
Fixed from v2
Earlier versions said iptables balances "round-robin". It does not: iptables and nftables pick a Pod at random per connection; only IPVS does true round-robin. See §6.1.

2. Architecture and workflows

2.1Architecture

In one sentenceFour places matter: your machine sends the YAML, the control plane stores it and lists Pods, every node holds the packet rules, and AWS adds load balancers and outside services.
PartWhere it runsReadsWritesOn Jahez EKS
kube-apiserver② control planeyour Service YAMLService + ClusterIP in etcdmanaged by AWS
etcd② control plane—every objectmanaged by AWS
EndpointSlice controller② kube-controller-managerServices + PodsEndpointSlicesmanaged by AWS
kube-proxy③ every node (DaemonSet)Services + EndpointSlicesiptables / IPVS / nftables rulesEKS add-on kube-proxy
CoreDNS③ kube-system (Deployment)Services + EndpointSlicesDNS answersEKS add-on coredns, ClusterIP 172.20.0.10
AWS Load Balancer Controller③ kube-system (Deployment)LoadBalancer ServicesNLB + status.loadBalancerHelm chart, IRSA role
VPC CNI③ every nodePodsPod IPs from VPC subnetsEKS add-on vpc-cni

DEPLOYMENTorder-api/order-api-deployment.yaml
In one sentenceRuns 3 order-api Pods labelled app: order-api with a container port named http — the two things the Service depends on.
YAMLorder-api-deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: order-api-deployment
  namespace: jahez-prod
  labels:
    app: order-api
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: order-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: order-api          # ← the Service selector matches this label
        tier: backend
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: order-api
          image: ghcr.io/jahez/order-api:2.14.0
          ports:
            - name: http          # ← Service targetPort: http points here
              containerPort: 8080
            - name: metrics
              containerPort: 9090
          readinessProbe:         # ← only Ready Pods receive Service traffic
            httpGet:
              path: /health/ready
              port: http
            periodSeconds: 5
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 250m
              memory: 256Mi
What each block does
  • template.metadata.labels.app — the label the Service selector matches.
  • ports[].name: http — the name the Service targetPort uses.
  • readinessProbe — decides when a Pod enters the EndpointSlice.

SERVICE · ClusterIPorder-api/order-api-service.yaml
In one sentenceGives the order-api Pods the name order-api-service and the stable IP 172.20.75.246, port 80 → container port http.
YAMLorder-api-service.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: order-api-service
  namespace: jahez-prod
  labels:
    app: order-api
spec:
  # ① Who receives traffic?
  selector:
    app: order-api
  # ② Which ports?
  ports:
    - # ① the API port
      name: http
      protocol: TCP
      appProtocol: http
      port: 80              # callers use order-api-service:80
      targetPort: http      # → containerPort named "http" (8080)
    - # ② the Prometheus port
      name: metrics
      protocol: TCP
      port: 9090
      targetPort: metrics
  # ③ Who can reach it?
  type: ClusterIP           # inside the cluster only
  # ④ How is traffic routed?
  internalTrafficPolicy: Cluster
  trafficDistribution: PreferClose   # prefer Pods in the caller's zone
What each block does
  • # ① Who receives traffic? — selector: app: order-api.
  • # ② Which ports? — http 80 → http and metrics 9090; both named because there are two.
  • # ③ Who can reach it? — ClusterIP: inside the cluster only.
  • # ④ How is traffic routed? — trafficDistribution: PreferClose keeps calls in the caller's zone.

STATEFULSETorders-db/orders-db-stateful-set.yaml
In one sentenceRuns 3 Postgres Pods with stable names and, through serviceName, a stable DNS name each.
YAMLorders-db-stateful-set.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: orders-db-stateful-set
  namespace: jahez-prod
  labels:
    app: orders-db
spec:
  serviceName: orders-db-headless-service   # ← gives each Pod a DNS name
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: orders-db
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: orders-db
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: postgres
          image: ghcr.io/jahez/postgres:16.4
          ports:
            - name: postgres
              containerPort: 5432
          volumeMounts:
            - name: data
              mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data
  volumeClaimTemplates:
    - metadata:
        name: data
      spec:
        accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
        storageClassName: gp3-storage-class
        resources:
          requests:
            storage: 100Gi
What each block does
  • serviceName must equal the headless Service name — it builds the Pod DNS names.
  • labels.app: orders-db — matched by the headless selector.
  • volumeClaimTemplates — one gp3 disk per replica (see the Storage guide).

SERVICE · Headlessorders-db/orders-db-headless-service.yaml
In one sentenceNo virtual IP: DNS returns each replica's own IP, and every replica gets the name <pod>.orders-db-headless-service.
YAMLorders-db-headless-service.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: orders-db-headless-service
  namespace: jahez-prod
  labels:
    app: orders-db
spec:
  # ① Who receives traffic?
  selector:
    app: orders-db
  publishNotReadyAddresses: true   # replicas must find each other before they are Ready
  # ② Which ports?
  ports:
    - # ① PostgreSQL
      name: postgres
      port: 5432
      targetPort: postgres
  # ③ Who can reach it?
  type: ClusterIP
  clusterIP: None                  # headless: no virtual IP, DNS returns Pod IPs
What each block does
  • clusterIP: None — headless; kube-proxy writes no rules for it.
  • publishNotReadyAddresses: true — replicas resolve each other before they are Ready (needed to form the cluster).
  • port 5432 → postgres — documented; clients connect to Pod IPs directly.

SERVICE · LoadBalancerstorefront-gateway/storefront-gateway-service.yaml
In one sentenceAsks the AWS Load Balancer Controller for an internet-facing NLB that sends HTTPS straight to the gateway Pod IPs.
YAMLstorefront-gateway-service.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: storefront-gateway-service
  namespace: jahez-prod
  labels:
    app: storefront-gateway
  annotations:
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-scheme: internet-facing
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-nlb-target-type: ip
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-cross-zone-load-balancing-enabled: "true"
spec:
  # ① Who receives traffic?
  selector:
    app: storefront-gateway
  # ② Which ports?
  ports:
    - # ① public HTTPS
      name: https
      protocol: TCP
      port: 443
      targetPort: https
  # ③ Who can reach it?
  type: LoadBalancer
  loadBalancerClass: service.k8s.aws/nlb    # AWS Load Balancer Controller builds an NLB
  loadBalancerSourceRanges:
    - 0.0.0.0/0
  allocateLoadBalancerNodePorts: false      # ip targets: NLB sends straight to Pod IPs
  # ④ How is traffic routed?
  externalTrafficPolicy: Local              # keep the client source IP
What each block does
  • annotations — tell the AWS controller: internet-facing, ip targets, cross-zone.
  • loadBalancerClass: service.k8s.aws/nlb — only the AWS controller acts on it.
  • allocateLoadBalancerNodePorts: false — no node ports, the NLB targets Pods.
  • externalTrafficPolicy: Local — keeps the customer source IP.
⌘ Commands for this file

SERVICE · NodePortops-debug/order-api-node-port-service.yaml
In one sentenceOpens port 30080 on every node so an engineer on the VPN can reach order-api through any node IP.
YAMLorder-api-node-port-service.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: order-api-node-port-service
  namespace: jahez-prod
  labels:
    app: order-api
    purpose: ops-debug
spec:
  # ① Who receives traffic?
  selector:
    app: order-api
  # ② Which ports?
  ports:
    - # ① debug entry on every node
      name: http
      port: 80
      targetPort: http
      nodePort: 30080       # open on every node: <node-ip>:30080
  # ③ Who can reach it?
  type: NodePort
  # ④ How is traffic routed?
  externalTrafficPolicy: Cluster
What each block does
  • nodePort: 30080 — fixed; must be free and in 30000-32767.
  • selector: app: order-api — the same Pods as the ClusterIP Service.
  • externalTrafficPolicy: Cluster — any node forwards to any Pod.

apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: loyalty-api-service
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  # ① Who receives traffic?  (no selector: you list the backends yourself)
  # ② Which ports?
  ports:
    - # ① the legacy API
      name: http
      protocol: TCP
      port: 80
      targetPort: 8080
  # ③ Who can reach it?
  type: ClusterIP
What each block does
  • No selector — the EndpointSlice controller ignores this Service.
  • ports[].name: http — must match the slice's port name.

kubectl apply -f apps/loyalty-legacy/loyalty-api-service.yaml

apiVersion: discovery.k8s.io/v1
kind: EndpointSlice
metadata:
  name: loyalty-api-endpoint-slice
  namespace: jahez-prod
  labels:
    kubernetes.io/service-name: loyalty-api-service     # ← links the slice to the Service
    endpointslice.kubernetes.io/managed-by: platform-team.jahez.net
# ① What kind of addresses?
addressType: IPv4
# ② Which port on them?
ports:
  - name: http          # must equal the Service port name
    protocol: TCP
    port: 8080
# ③ Which backends?
endpoints:
  - # ① legacy VM in me-central-1a
    addresses:
      - "10.0.96.21"
    conditions:
      ready: true
    zone: me-central-1a
  - # ② legacy VM in me-central-1b
    addresses:
      - "10.0.112.34"
    conditions:
      ready: true
    zone: me-central-1b
What each block does
  • kubernetes.io/service-name label — links it to the Service.
  • managed-by label — any value except the controller's own.
  • endpoints[].zone — lets zone-aware routing work for VMs too.

2.3Internal order

In one sentenceOne apply travels through seven stages: kubectl sends it, the API server checks it, allocates the IP and stores it, then three watchers — the EndpointSlice controller, kube-proxy and CoreDNS — each build their part.

Traced with kubectl apply -f apps/order-api/order-api-service.yaml. Each stage shows ① Input → ② Logic → ③ Output; tap any row to open the full object. Stages 0-4 are real (kube-apiserver v1.34.1); 5-7 show what the controller, kube-proxy and CoreDNS write in a running cluster.

Stage 0 · run
Whereyour machine / CIBlockscommand + fileCommandkubectl apply -f apps/order-api/order-api-service.yaml
What happens

You (or a CI job, or Argo CD) run kubectl apply with the file path. kubectl reads the file from disk and finds the cluster in ~/.kube/config (context jahez-prod-eks). If the path is wrong it stops here: error: the path "apps/order-api/order-api-svc.yaml" does not exist.

NEW · read now
→↓
② LOGIC · kubeconfig
current-context: jahez-prod-eks

Which cluster and which user the request goes to.

→↓
③ OUTPUT · in memory RAM
1 new · 0 changed
📌 Remember
Nothing reached the cluster yet. A wrong context means you apply to the wrong cluster — check kubectl config current-context.
← Prev1 / 8
Stage 1 · request
Whereyour machineBlockskubectlCommandkubectl apply …
What happens

kubectl parses the YAML, adds the last-applied-configuration annotation (used to compute future diffs), and sends an HTTPS POST (create) or PATCH (update) to the API server.

Where② control planeBlocksIP allocatorCommand—

Because type: ClusterIP and no clusterIP was given, the API server reserves a free address from the Service range 172.20.0.0/16: 172.20.75.246. For NodePort/LoadBalancer it also reserves a node port.

Stage 5 · EndpointSlice
Where② kube-controller-managerBlocksEndpointSlice controllerCommandkubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=order-api-service
What happens

The controller sees the new Service, finds every Pod in jahez-prod whose labels match the selector, resolves the named targetPort: http to each Pod's containerPort 8080, reads readiness, and writes one EndpointSlice. Zone hints are added because of trafficDistribution.

NEW · read now

→↓

1 new
📌 Remember
A selector that matches nothing is not an error — the slice is simply empty. Always check it after a deploy.
6 / 8
Stage 6 · kube-proxy
Where③ every nodeBlockskube-proxyCommandsudo iptables-save -t nat | grep order-api
What happens

kube-proxy on every node gets the Service and the slice. It writes one rule that matches 172.20.75.246:80 and one DNAT rule per Ready endpoint, each chosen with a random probability. With PreferClose, a node in me-central-1a only uses endpoints hinted for 1a (fallback: all).

1 new chain · 3 endpoints
📌 Remember
Rules are per node. If one node's kube-proxy is broken, only Pods on that node see stale backends.
7 / 8
Stage 7 · CoreDNS
Where③ kube-systemBlocksCoreDNSCommandnslookup order-api-service
What happens

CoreDNS watches Services and slices too. It now answers the A record order-api-service.jahez-prod.svc.cluster.local → 172.20.75.246 and an SRV record for each named port.

Wherenode-a kernelBlockskube-proxy rulesCommandsudo iptables-save -t nat | grep 172.20.75.246
  • The packet leaves the Pod and hits node-a's nat table before any routing.

  • With PreferClose, node-a (me-central-1a) only has the 1a endpoint in its chain.

Part II · Low Level

3. Service object

3.0How a Service works

In one sentenceA Service answers four questions — who receives traffic, on which ports, who can reach it, and how each connection is routed — and Kubernetes writes the rest.
🧠 The logic, read first
Question it answersFieldsThink of it as
① Who receives traffic?selector · publishNotReadyAddressesthe guest list: which Pods may answer
② Which ports?ports[]the switchboard: extension 80 rings desk 8080
③ Who can reach it?type · clusterIP · externalName · loadBalancer*the front door: internal only, node door, cloud door, or a forwarding address
④ How is traffic routed?externalTrafficPolicy · internalTrafficPolicy · trafficDistribution · sessionAffinitythe usher: nearest Pod, local Pod, same Pod again
Written by KubernetesclusterIP · nodePort · statusthe receipt you get back
API groupcore · v1
Scopenamespaced
Livesuntil deleted
Short namesvc
Typical count1 per app, + extras

Structure

Service
├─ metadata ............ name · namespace · labels · annotations (cloud settings)
└─ spec
   ├─ ① Who receives traffic?   selector · publishNotReadyAddresses
   ├─ ② Which ports?            ports[]: name · protocol · appProtocol · port · targetPort · nodePort
   ├─ ③ Who can reach it?       type · clusterIP(s) · ipFamilies · ipFamilyPolicy · externalIPs
   │                            externalName · loadBalancerClass · loadBalancerSourceRanges
   │                            allocateLoadBalancerNodePorts
   └─ ④ How is traffic routed?  externalTrafficPolicy · healthCheckNodePort · internalTrafficPolicy
                                sessionAffinity · sessionAffinityConfig · trafficDistribution
status (written by Kubernetes) . loadBalancer.ingress[] · conditions[]

One full YAML using every field

YAMLstorefront-gateway-full-service.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: storefront-gateway-full-service
  namespace: jahez-prod
  labels:
    app: storefront-gateway
  annotations:
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-scheme: internet-facing
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-nlb-target-type: ip
spec:
  # ① Who receives traffic?
  selector:
    app: storefront-gateway
  publishNotReadyAddresses: false
  # ② Which ports?
  ports:
    - # ① public HTTPS
      name: https
      protocol: TCP
      appProtocol: https
      port: 443
      targetPort: https
      nodePort: 31443
  # ③ Who can reach it?
  type: LoadBalancer
  clusterIP: 172.20.140.10
  clusterIPs:
    - 172.20.140.10
  ipFamilyPolicy: SingleStack
  ipFamilies:
    - IPv4
  externalIPs: []              # keep empty — see the trap in §3.3
  loadBalancerClass: service.k8s.aws/nlb
  loadBalancerSourceRanges:
    - 0.0.0.0/0
  allocateLoadBalancerNodePorts: true
  # ④ How is traffic routed?
  externalTrafficPolicy: Local
  healthCheckNodePort: 32100
  internalTrafficPolicy: Cluster
  sessionAffinity: ClientIP
  sessionAffinityConfig:
    clientIP:
      timeoutSeconds: 10800
  trafficDistribution: PreferClose
# ── Written by Kubernetes (never write it yourself) ──
# status:
#   loadBalancer:
#     ingress:
#       - hostname: k8s-jahezpro-storefro-….elb.me-central-1.amazonaws.com
Two fields not shown
externalName only exists on type: ExternalName (§3.7). loadBalancerIP is deprecated since v1.24 — use the cloud's annotation instead.

3.1① Who receives traffic?

In one sentenceThe selector is a label filter: every Pod in the namespace with those labels — and Ready — becomes a backend, re-evaluated continuously.
🧠 The logic, read first
Question it answersFieldsThink of it as
Which Pods?selectora guest list by badge colour
Before they are Ready too?publishNotReadyAddresseslet guests in while they are still at the door
YAMLorder-api-deployment-and-service.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: order-api-deployment
  namespace: jahez-prod
  labels:
    app: order-api
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: order-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: order-api          # ← the Service selector matches this label
        tier: backend
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: order-api
          image: ghcr.io/jahez/order-api:2.14.0
          ports:
            - name: http          # ← Service targetPort: http points here
              containerPort: 8080
            - name: metrics
              containerPort: 9090
          readinessProbe:         # ← only Ready Pods receive Service traffic
            httpGet:
              path: /health/ready
              port: http
            periodSeconds: 5
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 250m
              memory: 256Mi
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: order-api-service
  namespace: jahez-prod
  labels:
    app: order-api
spec:
  # ① Who receives traffic?
  selector:
    app: order-api
  # ② Which ports?
  ports:
    - # ① the API port
      name: http
      protocol: TCP
      appProtocol: http
      port: 80              # callers use order-api-service:80
      targetPort: http      # → containerPort named "http" (8080)
    - # ② the Prometheus port
      name: metrics
      protocol: TCP
      port: 9090
      targetPort: metrics
  # ③ Who can reach it?
  type: ClusterIP           # inside the cluster only
  # ④ How is traffic routed?
  internalTrafficPolicy: Cluster
  trafficDistribution: PreferClose   # prefer Pods in the caller's zone

3.2② Which ports?

In one sentenceEach port entry maps what callers dial (port) to where the Pod listens (targetPort), optionally through a port on every node (nodePort).
🧠 The logic, read first
Question it answersFieldsThink of it as
What do callers dial?port · protocolthe extension number
Where does it land?targetPortthe desk phone
Which door on the nodes?nodePortthe building's side entrance

YAMLorder-api-service-ports.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: order-api-service
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  # ① Who receives traffic?
  selector:
    app: order-api
  # ② Which ports?
  ports:
    - # ① the API — by name, survives a container port change
      name: http
      protocol: TCP
      appProtocol: http
      port: 80
      targetPort: http
    - # ② Prometheus scraping — by number
      name: metrics
      protocol: TCP
      port: 9090
      targetPort: 9090
    - # ③ gRPC for internal callers
      name: grpc
      protocol: TCP
      appProtocol: kubernetes.io/h2c
      port: 5000
      targetPort: 5000
  # ③ Who can reach it?
  type: ClusterIP

The Service says targetPort: http; each Pod says containerPort: 8080, name: http. When order-api 3.0 moves to 8081, you change only the Deployment — the Service keeps working during the rollout because old Pods resolve to 8080 and new ones to 8081.

targetPort: 8080 is simpler but couples Service and image. Changing the image port means changing both at the same time.

Every entry needs a unique name. Real error with two unnamed ports:

3.4Headless (clusterIP: None)

In one sentenceA headless Service has no virtual IP: DNS returns the Pods' own IPs, and with a StatefulSet each Pod gets its own stable name.
🧠 The logic, read first
Question it answersFieldsThink of it as
No virtual IP?clusterIP: Nonea phone book instead of a switchboard
Which Pods are listed?selector · publishNotReadyAddresseseveryone, even those still arriving
Per-Pod names?StatefulSet.serviceNamename tags on each desk
ClusterIPNone
kube-proxyignores it
Balancingthe client
Jahez useorders-db, Kafka, Redis
YAMLorders-db-headless-service-and-stateful-set.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: orders-db-headless-service
  namespace: jahez-prod
  labels:
    app: orders-db
spec:
  # ① Who receives traffic?
  selector:
    app: orders-db
  publishNotReadyAddresses: true   # replicas must find each other before they are Ready
  # ② Which ports?
  ports:
    - # ① PostgreSQL
      name: postgres
      port: 5432
      targetPort: postgres
  # ③ Who can reach it?
  type: ClusterIP
  clusterIP: None                  # headless: no virtual IP, DNS returns Pod IPs
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: orders-db-stateful-set
  namespace: jahez-prod
  labels:
    app: orders-db
spec:
  serviceName: orders-db-headless-service   # ← gives each Pod a DNS name
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: orders-db
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: orders-db
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: postgres
          image: ghcr.io/jahez/postgres:16.4
          ports:
            - name: postgres
              containerPort: 5432
          volumeMounts:
            - name: data
              mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data
  volumeClaimTemplates:
    - metadata:
        name: data
      spec:
        accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
        storageClassName: gp3-storage-class
        resources:
          requests:
            storage: 100Gi

Deep dive → Packet paths
healthCheckNodePortintwith Local: port where the LB checks "do you have a local Pod?"

Allocated automatically; the cloud LB marks nodes without local Pods unhealthy.

Deep dive — Cluster vs Local

node-c has no order-api Pod. A request to node-c:30080 is forwarded to a Pod on node-a, and the source IP is rewritten to node-c (SNAT) so the reply comes back the same way. Even spread, one extra hop, client IP lost.

Only Pods on the receiving node answer. The client IP is kept. A node with no local Pod drops the packet — the load balancer must skip it via healthCheckNodePort.

ClusterLocal
Client source IPlost (SNAT)kept
Extra hoppossiblenever
Nodes without Podsstill workdrop traffic
Spreadeven across Podseven across nodes — uneven per Pod
Jahez usedebug NodePortpublic NLB (fraud checks need client IP)

3.6LoadBalancer

In one sentenceLoadBalancer asks a cloud controller for an external load balancer — on Jahez EKS an AWS NLB built by the AWS Load Balancer Controller — and writes its hostname back into the Service.
🧠 The logic, read first
Question it answersFieldsThink of it as
Which controller?loadBalancerClasswhich contractor builds the door
Who may enter?loadBalancerSourceRangesthe guest list at the gate
Through nodes or straight to Pods?allocateLoadBalancerNodePorts · annotationsside door or direct corridor
Where is it?status.loadBalancerthe address on the receipt
Builds1 NLB per Service
Ready after~2-3 min
Costper NLB + LCU
Jahez usestorefront-gateway
YAMLstorefront-gateway-service.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: storefront-gateway-service
  namespace: jahez-prod
  labels:
    app: storefront-gateway
  annotations:
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-scheme: internet-facing
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-nlb-target-type: ip
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-cross-zone-load-balancing-enabled: "true"
spec:
  # ① Who receives traffic?
  selector:
    app: storefront-gateway
  # ② Which ports?
  ports:
    - # ① public HTTPS
      name: https
      protocol: TCP
      port: 443
      targetPort: https
  # ③ Who can reach it?
  type: LoadBalancer
  loadBalancerClass: service.k8s.aws/nlb    # AWS Load Balancer Controller builds an NLB
  loadBalancerSourceRanges:
    - 0.0.0.0/0
  allocateLoadBalancerNodePorts: false      # ip targets: NLB sends straight to Pod IPs
  # ④ How is traffic routed?
  externalTrafficPolicy: Local              # keep the client source IP

Deep dive — instance vs ip targets

The NLB sends to node-ip:nodePort; kube-proxy forwards to a Pod (maybe on another node). Needs node ports.

The NLB sends straight to Pod IPs (the controller watches EndpointSlices and updates the target group). No node hop, no node ports needed. Jahez default.

instanceip
NLB targetnode:nodePortPod IP:targetPort
Extra hoppossiblenone
Needs node ports✓✕ (set allocateLoadBalancerNodePorts: false)
Target updatesnode listevery Pod change
Fargate Pods✕✓

3.8④ How is traffic routed?

In one sentenceFour fields steer which Pod gets a new connection: stickiness per client, node-local only, zone-close first, and — for outside traffic — local Pods only.
🧠 The logic, read first
Question it answersFieldsThink of it as
Same caller, same Pod?sessionAffinity · sessionAffinityConfiga regular table at the café
Only this node?internalTrafficPolicystay in the building
Same zone first?trafficDistributionnearest branch first
Outside callers?externalTrafficPolicysee §3.5
YAMLmenu-cache-service.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: menu-cache-service
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  # ① Who receives traffic?
  selector:
    app: menu-cache
  # ② Which ports?
  ports:
    - # ① cache API
      name: http
      port: 80
      targetPort: 8080
  # ③ Who can reach it?
  type: ClusterIP
  # ④ How is traffic routed?
  sessionAffinity: ClientIP          # same caller Pod → same cache Pod
  sessionAffinityConfig:
    clientIP:
      timeoutSeconds: 600
  internalTrafficPolicy: Cluster
  trafficDistribution: PreferSameZone  # keep calls inside the caller's AZ
⌘ Commands for this file

4. EndpointSlices

4.0How an EndpointSlice works

In one sentenceAn EndpointSlice is the live list of backend addresses for one Service — written by the controller, read by kube-proxy, CoreDNS and load balancer controllers.
🧠 The logic, read first
Question it answersFieldsThink of it as
Which Service?kubernetes.io/service-namethe folder label
① What kind of addresses?addressTypeIPv4 or IPv6 pages
② Which ports?ports[]resolved door numbers
③ Which backends?endpoints[]one line per Pod with its state
API groupdiscovery.k8s.io/v1
Per Service1+ slices
Size≤100 endpoints
Writercontroller (or you)
YAMLorder-api-service-7xk2p.yaml (as written by the controller)
apiVersion: discovery.k8s.io/v1
kind: EndpointSlice
metadata:
  name: order-api-service-7xk2p
  namespace: jahez-prod
  labels:
    kubernetes.io/service-name: order-api-service                       # ← which Service
    endpointslice.kubernetes.io/managed-by: endpointslice-controller.k8s.io # ← who writes it
# ① What kind of addresses?
addressType: IPv4
# ② Which ports on them?
ports:
  - name: http          # same name as the Service port
    protocol: TCP
    port: 8080          # targetPort "http" resolved
    appProtocol: http
  - name: metrics
    protocol: TCP
    port: 9090
# ③ Which backends?
endpoints:
  - # ① Pod in me-central-1a
    addresses:
      - "10.0.41.23"
    conditions:
      ready: true
      serving: true
      terminating: false
    nodeName: ip-10-0-41-17.me-central-1.compute.internal
    zone: me-central-1a
    hints:
      forZones:
        - name: me-central-1a
    targetRef:
      kind: Pod
      namespace: jahez-prod
      name: order-api-deployment-7d9f8c6b5-x2kqp
  - # ② Pod in me-central-1b
    addresses:
      - "10.0.77.140"
    conditions:
      ready: true
      serving: true
      terminating: false
    nodeName: ip-10-0-77-52.me-central-1.compute.internal
    zone: me-central-1b
    hints:
      forZones:
        - name: me-central-1b
    targetRef:
      kind: Pod
      namespace: jahez-prod
      name: order-api-deployment-7d9f8c6b5-m8w4t

4.1Conditions: ready · serving · terminating

In one sentenceEach endpoint carries three flags; kube-proxy sends new connections only to ready ones, and uses serving-but-terminating Pods only when nothing else is left.
FlagMeanskube-proxy does
ready: truePod Ready and not terminatingnew connections go here
serving: truereadiness passes (even while terminating)used only if no ready endpoint exists (graceful fallback)
terminating: truePod has a deletionTimestampno new connections; existing ones finish

Lifecycle of one endpoint during a rollout

Step 1 / 4 · Pod starts
Wherekubelet → controllerBlocksEndpointSliceCommandkubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=order-api-service -n jahez-prod -o wide
  • A new Pod from the rollout gets IP 10.0.41.57 on node-a.
  • Its readinessProbe has not passed yet, so it is listed as not ready.
  • kube-proxy does not send it traffic.

What removes an endpoint

EventEffect on the sliceTraffic
Readiness failsready: falsestops until it passes again
Pod deleted / evicted / drainedterminating: true → removeddrains, then gone
Label changed on the Podremoved immediatelycut at once — useful to take a Pod out for debugging

Node NotReadyPods marked not ready after eviction timeoutstops
Service deletedslices garbage-collected (ownerReference)ClusterIP stops working
YAMLorder-api-deployment.yaml (the readinessProbe drives ready)
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: order-api-deployment
  namespace: jahez-prod
  labels:
    app: order-api
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: order-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: order-api          # ← the Service selector matches this label
        tier: backend
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: order-api
          image: ghcr.io/jahez/order-api:2.14.0
          ports:
            - name: http          # ← Service targetPort: http points here
              containerPort: 8080
            - name: metrics
              containerPort: 9090
          readinessProbe:         # ← only Ready Pods receive Service traffic
            httpGet:
              path: /health/ready
              port: http
            periodSeconds: 5
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 250m
              memory: 256Mi

4.2Zones & topology hints

In one sentenceWith trafficDistribution (or the older topology-mode annotation), the controller adds zone hints so each node prefers endpoints in its own AZ — lower latency and no cross-AZ data charges.
🧠 The logic, read first
Question it answersFieldsThink of it as
Should zones matter?spec.trafficDistributionprefer the nearest branch
Which zone is an endpoint for?endpoints[].hints.forZonesa sticker per Pod
Older switchservice.kubernetes.io/topology-mode: Autobalances hints by CPU per zone; may skip hints
YAMLslice with zone hints (part)
apiVersion: discovery.k8s.io/v1
kind: EndpointSlice
metadata:
  name: order-api-service-7xk2p
  namespace: jahez-prod
  labels:
    kubernetes.io/service-name: order-api-service                       # ← which Service
    endpointslice.kubernetes.io/managed-by: endpointslice-controller.k8s.io # ← who writes it
# ① What kind of addresses?
addressType: IPv4
# ② Which ports on them?
ports:
  - name: http          # same name as the Service port
    protocol: TCP
    port: 8080          # targetPort "http" resolved
    appProtocol: http
  - name: metrics
    protocol: TCP
    port: 9090
# ③ Which backends?
endpoints:
  - # ① Pod in me-central-1a
    addresses:
      - "10.0.41.23"
    conditions:
      ready: true
      serving: true
      terminating: false
    nodeName: ip-10-0-41-17.me-central-1.compute.internal
    zone: me-central-1a
    hints:
      forZones:
        - name: me-central-1a
    targetRef:
      kind: Pod
      namespace: jahez-prod
      name: order-api-deployment-7d9f8c6b5-x2kqp
⚠ Watch out
  • Hints need Pods in every zone. With 3 replicas and one zone down, a zone may get no local endpoint → fallback to all zones.
  • PreferClose can overload a zone that has most callers but few Pods — spread replicas with topologySpreadConstraints.
③ Every property — tap to open
hintsobjectrouting hints per endpoint
•forZones[].namestringzone that should use this endpoint
•forNodes[].namestringnode that should use it (PreferSameNode, v1.34+)

4.3Services without a selector

In one sentenceLeave out the selector and write the EndpointSlice yourself: the Service gets a ClusterIP and DNS name, but its backends can be anything with an IP — here two legacy EC2 VMs.
🧠 The logic, read first
Question it answersFieldsThink of it as
Who lists backends?(no selector) · managed-byyou keep the guest list
How is it linked?kubernetes.io/service-namethe folder label
Which port?ports[].namemust equal the Service port name
YAMLloyalty-api-service-and-endpoint-slice.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: loyalty-api-service
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  # ① Who receives traffic?  (no selector: you list the backends yourself)
  # ② Which ports?
  ports:
    - # ① the legacy API
      name: http
      protocol: TCP
      port: 80
      targetPort: 8080
  # ③ Who can reach it?
  type: ClusterIP
---
apiVersion: discovery.k8s.io/v1
kind: EndpointSlice
metadata:
  name: loyalty-api-endpoint-slice
  namespace: jahez-prod
  labels:
    kubernetes.io/service-name: loyalty-api-service     # ← links the slice to the Service
    endpointslice.kubernetes.io/managed-by: platform-team.jahez.net
# ① What kind of addresses?
addressType: IPv4
# ② Which port on them?
ports:
  - name: http          # must equal the Service port name
    protocol: TCP
    port: 8080
# ③ Which backends?
endpoints:
  - # ① legacy VM in me-central-1a
    addresses:
      - "10.0.96.21"
    conditions:
      ready: true
    zone: me-central-1a
  - # ② legacy VM in me-central-1b
    addresses:
      - "10.0.112.34"
    conditions:
      ready: true
    zone: me-central-1b

If you still have hand-written Endpoints
The EndpointSlice mirroring controller copies custom Endpoints (for selector-less Services) into slices, so old manifests keep working. Write slices for anything new.

5. Service DNS

5.0How Service DNS works

In one sentenceCoreDNS watches Services and EndpointSlices and answers names under cluster.local; every Pod's resolv.conf points at CoreDNS and adds search domains so short names work.
RecordNameAnswer
A / AAAAorder-api-service.jahez-prod.svc.cluster.localClusterIP 172.20.75.246
A (headless)orders-db-headless-service.jahez-prod.svc.cluster.localevery ready Pod IP
A (per Pod)orders-db-stateful-set-0.orders-db-headless-service…that Pod's IP
SRV_http._tcp.order-api-service.jahez-prod.svc.cluster.localport 80 + target name
CNAMEpayments-db-service.jahez-prod.svc.cluster.localthe externalName
PTR246.75.20.172.in-addr.arpathe Service name
YAMLcoredns ConfigMap (EKS add-on, kube-system)
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: coredns
  namespace: kube-system
data:
  Corefile: |
    .:53 {
        errors
        health {
            lameduck 5s
        }
        ready
        kubernetes cluster.local in-addr.arpa ip6.arpa {
            pods insecure
            fallthrough in-addr.arpa ip6.arpa
        }
        prometheus :9153
        forward . /etc/resolv.conf
        cache 30
        loop
        reload
        loadbalance
    }

5.3Pod DNS settings & ndots

In one sentencednsPolicy chooses which resolver a Pod uses; dnsConfig tunes it — and ndots:5 is why calls to external APIs can make five DNS lookups first.
🧠 The logic, read first
Question it answersFieldsThink of it as
Which resolver?dnsPolicywhich phone book
TuningdnsConfig.options · nameservers · searcheshow hard to search before dialling directly
YAMLcheckout-api-deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: checkout-api-deployment
  namespace: jahez-prod
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: checkout-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: checkout-api
    spec:
      dnsPolicy: ClusterFirst          # use CoreDNS (default)
      dnsConfig:
        options:
          - name: ndots
            value: "2"                 # api.moyasar.com resolves on the first try
          - name: single-request-reopen
      containers:
        - name: checkout-api
          image: ghcr.io/jahez/checkout-api:4.3.2
          ports:
            - name: http
              containerPort: 8080

5.4Names across namespaces

In one sentenceShort names only resolve inside the same namespace; from anywhere else add the namespace, and in config prefer the full name.
Name usedFrom jahez-prodFrom jahez-stagingFrom kube-system

⚠ Watch out
Using the short name in shared config makes staging silently call staging (good) — or nothing (bad) if the Service only exists in prod. Name the namespace when crossing it on purpose.

6. kube-proxy & data plane

6.0How kube-proxy works

In one sentencekube-proxy runs on every node, watches Services and EndpointSlices, and rewrites the kernel's packet rules so a ClusterIP or NodePort becomes a real Pod address.
🧠 The logic, read first
Question it answersFieldsThink of it as
① Which engine?modewhich switchboard model
② What is inside?clusterCIDRwhich callers need no masquerade
③ How often?syncPeriod · minSyncPeriodhow fast the list is redrawn
④ Which node IPs?nodePortAddresseswhich doors get NodePorts
⑤ Flow memoryconntrack.*the call log
YAMLkube-proxy-config (EKS add-on, kube-system)
apiVersion: kubeproxy.config.k8s.io/v1alpha1
kind: KubeProxyConfiguration
# ① Which engine?
mode: iptables                 # iptables · ipvs · nftables
# ② Which traffic is "inside"?
clusterCIDR: 10.0.0.0/16       # Pod range (VPC CIDR on EKS)
# ③ How often to rewrite rules?
iptables:
  masqueradeAll: false
  syncPeriod: 30s
  minSyncPeriod: 1s
ipvs:
  scheduler: rr                # only used when mode: ipvs
nftables:
  syncPeriod: 30s
  minSyncPeriod: 1s
# ④ Which node addresses accept NodePorts?
nodePortAddresses:
  - primary
# ⑤ Connection tracking
conntrack:
  maxPerCore: 32768
  min: 131072
  tcpEstablishedTimeout: 24h0m0s
  tcpCloseWaitTimeout: 1h0m0s
metricsBindAddress: 0.0.0.0:10249

6.1iptables mode

In one sentenceIn iptables mode each Service is a chain of rules; each endpoint is chosen with a random probability, so every new connection lands on a random Ready Pod — not round-robin.

The probabilities are chained: 1/3, then 1/2 of the remaining 2/3, then all the rest → each Pod gets exactly 1/3 on average.

CMDbash
sudo iptables-save -t nat | grep -E "order-api-service|HMBXK3VY"

-A KUBE-SVC-HMBXK3VY6A3W2RQM -m comment --comment "jahez-prod/order-api-service:http -> 10.0.77.140:8080" -m statistic --mode random --probability 0.50000000000 -j KUBE-SEP-NM2QL7R3G4ZXW8TB
-A KUBE-SVC-HMBXK3VY6A3W2RQM -m comment --comment "jahez-prod/order-api-service:http -> 10.0.118.9:8080" -j KUBE-SEP-QS7D5HZ6P2JXK3UA
-A KUBE-SEP-2YQK5MDUFXX4RJ7C -p tcp -m comment --comment "jahez-prod/order-api-service:http" -m tcp -j DNAT --to-destination 10.0.41.23:8080
Fixed from v2
v2 said iptables balances "round-robin" in two places. It picks at random per connection; long-lived connections (gRPC, HTTP/2, DB pools) stay on the Pod they first got.

6.2IPVS mode

In one sentenceIPVS is a kernel load balancer with hash-table lookups and real schedulers (round-robin by default); kube-proxy also binds every ClusterIP to a dummy interface, so ClusterIPs answer ping.
CMDbash
sudo ipvsadm -Ln -t 172.20.75.246:80
OUTExample outputexample — needs running Pods
Prot LocalAddress:Port Scheduler Flags
  -> RemoteAddress:Port           Forward Weight ActiveConn InActConn
TCP  172.20.75.246:80 rr
  -> 10.0.41.23:8080              Masq    1      14         3
  -> 10.0.77.140:8080             Masq    1      13         2
  -> 10.0.118.9:8080              Masq    1      14         4
schedulerPicks
rrnext Pod in turn (default)
lcfewest active connections
shhash of source IP (sticky)
wrr / wlcweighted variants

6.3nftables mode

In one sentencenftables mode (GA in v1.33) replaces long iptables chains with maps: lookups stay fast and updates are incremental, which matters at thousands of Services.
CMDbash
sudo nft list map ip kube-proxy service-ips
OUTExample outputexample — needs running Pods
table ip kube-proxy {
	map service-ips {
		type ipv4_addr . inet_proto . inet_service : verdict
		elements = { 172.20.75.246 . tcp . 80 : goto service-HMBXK3VY-jahez-prod/order-api-service/tcp/http,
			     172.20.0.10 . udp . 53 : goto service-TCOU7JCQ-kube-system/kube-dns/udp/dns }
	}
}
⚠ Watch out
  • Needs a recent kernel (5.13+) and a kube-proxy build that supports it — check the EKS add-on version before switching.
  • Like iptables mode, it picks endpoints at random per connection.

6.4Packet paths

In one sentenceThe same ClusterIP call takes different paths depending on where the chosen Pod runs, and NodePort traffic depends on externalTrafficPolicy.

menu-api and the chosen order-api Pod are both on node-a: DNAT then straight across the node's virtual interfaces — no network hop.

The chosen Pod is on node-b. After DNAT the packet is a normal Pod-to-Pod packet: on EKS the VPC routes the Pod IP (it is a secondary IP on node-b's ENI); other CNIs use VXLAN or BGP. The reply is un-NATed on node-a by conntrack.

Arrives at node-b:30080, forwarded to any Pod; source NAT to node-b so the reply returns through it. Client IP lost.

The NLB sends directly to a Pod IP — kube-proxy is not on the path. Client IP preserved by the NLB.

Two Pods never share an IP
Every Pod IP is unique in the cluster: on EKS each one is a distinct VPC address; on overlay CNIs each node owns its own Pod CIDR block (e.g. a /24), so blocks never overlap.

7. Commands

In one sentenceEvery Service command is kubectl VERB TYPE[/NAME] plus verb flags and a namespace — learn the slots once and every card below reads the same.

<PLACEHOLDER> = you fill it · [optional] = may be left out · green = type exactly.

7.1kubectl expose

In one sentenceCreate a Service from an existing Deployment, ReplicaSet, Pod or Service, copying its selector and port.

kubectl expose

Build a Service whose selector comes from the workload — the fastest correct way in the CKAD.

kubectl reads order-api-deployment from the API server, copies spec.selector.matchLabels (app: order-api) into a new Service and sends it back.

CMDbash
kubectl expose deployment order-api-deployment --name=order-api-service --port=80 --target-port=http -n jahez-prod --dry-run=client -o yaml
💡 Command hint
build the object locally→print it→nothing sent — cluster unchanged

Generate the YAML on your machine; the cluster never sees it.

kubectlthe Kubernetes CLI; every call talks to the API server of the current context
exposebuild a Service whose selector and ports are copied from an existing object
deploymentthe resource type: a Deployment
order-api-deploymentobject name
--name=order-api-servicename of the new Service → order-api-service
--port=80the Service port callers use → 80
--target-port=httpthe Pod port traffic goes to (number or name) → http
-nnamespace to work in
jahez-prodJahez production namespace
--dry-run=clientbuild the object locally and stop — nothing is sent
-ooutput format (wide, yaml, json, jsonpath, name)
yamlargument
OUTOutputreal output · kube-apiserver v1.34.1

kind: Service

    app: order-api

A Service whose selector is app: order-api — copied, not typed, so it matches.

Error from server (AlreadyExists): services "order-api-service" already exists — the name is taken; pick another or delete the old one.

In one sentenceCreate a Service of a given type from flags only — no workload needed, but it invents a selector app=<service-name> that you almost always must fix.

Everything comes from your flags. With --dry-run=client kubectl only prints YAML — the cluster never sees it.

7.4Change & delete: patch · set selector · delete

In one sentenceChange a live Service in place with patch or set selector; delete removes it and, for LoadBalancer, its cloud load balancer.

kubectl patch svc

Change some fields of a live Service.

Sends only the changed fields; the API server merges and validates them.

CMDbash
kubectl patch svc order-api-service -n jahez-prod --type=merge -p '{"spec":{"trafficDistribution":"PreferSameZone"}}'
💡 Command hint
send the object to the API server→validate + store in etcd→controllers react

Change the cluster: the API server stores it and controllers build the rest.

kubectlthe Kubernetes CLI; every call talks to the API server of the current context
patchchange some fields of a live object in place
svcshort name for Service
order-api-serviceobject name
-nnamespace to work in
jahez-prodJahez production namespace
--type=mergeJSON merge patch: the given fields replace the live ones
-pargument
'{"spec":{"trafficDistribution":"PreferSameZone"}}'the patch body (JSON)
OUTExample outputexample — needs running Pods
service/order-api-service patched
✓ Result
Every node's kube-proxy re-reads the Service within a second.
✕ When it fails
The Service "order-api-service" is invalid: spec.clusterIPs[0]: Invalid value: ["172.20.0.50"]: may not change once set

Remove a Service; its slices, rules, DNS record and cloud LB go with it.

The API server deletes the object (after finalizers clear); controllers remove everything derived from it.

💡 Command hint
send to the API server→validate + default→nothing saved

Ask the API server to check the object without saving it.

deleteremove the object; the controllers clean up what it owned
svcshort name for Service

service "loyalty-api-service" deleted from jahez-prod namespace (server dry run)
✓ Result

✕ When it fails
Stuck in Terminating → the finalizer's controller is down; fix it rather than removing the finalizer.

kubectl delete svc <NAME>|-l <SELECTOR> [-n <NAMESPACE>] [--dry-run=server]
Parameters
ParameterMeaningSample valuesExample
NAMEServiceorder-api-node-port-servicekubectl delete svc order-api-node-port-service -n jahez-prod

  • Deleting and recreating gives a new ClusterIP — clients caching the IP break; DNS users recover.

7.5Reach & test: port-forward · run

In one sentenceport-forward reaches a Service from your laptop without exposing it; a throwaway Pod tests DNS and HTTP from inside the cluster, like a real caller.

kubectl port-forward

Tunnel a local port through the API server to one Pod behind the Service.

kubectl picks one Pod behind the Service and tunnels to it via the API server and kubelet. kube-proxy is not used — no load balancing.

CMDbash
kubectl port-forward svc/order-api-service 8080:80 -n jahez-prod
💡 Command hint
tunnel through the API server→kubelet → one Pod→localhost reaches it→nothing created

Reach one Pod behind the Service from your laptop, without exposing anything.

kubectlthe Kubernetes CLI; every call talks to the API server of the current context
port-forwardopen a local port that tunnels through the API server to one Pod
svc/order-api-servicethe object to act on, as TYPE/NAME
8080:80LOCAL:REMOTE ports (local port → Service port)
-nnamespace to work in
jahez-prodJahez production namespace
OUTExample outputexample — needs running Pods
Forwarding from 127.0.0.1:8080 -> 8080
Forwarding from [::1]:8080 -> 8080
Handling connection for 8080
✓ Result
curl localhost:8080/health on your laptop hits one order-api Pod.
✕ When it fails
error: timed out waiting for the condition — no running Pod behind the Service (the lab cluster has none).
Template
kubectl port-forward <svc/NAME> [<LOCAL>:]<REMOTE> [-n <NAMESPACE>] [--address <IP>]
Parameters
ParameterMeaningSample valuesExample
svc/NAME requiredService (or pod/, deploy/)svc/order-api-servicepod/order-api-deployment-7d9f8c6b5-x2kqpkubectl port-forward svc/order-api-service 8080:80 -n jahez-prod
LOCAL:REMOTE requiredlaptop port : Service port8080:80:80 (random local)kubectl port-forward svc/orders-db-headless-service 15432:5432 -n jahez-prod
--addresslisten address127.0.0.10.0.0.0kubectl port-forward svc/order-api-service 8080:80 --address 0.0.0.0 -n jahez-prod
Watch out
  • Stays on one Pod until restarted.
  • REMOTE is the Service port; kubectl maps it to the targetPort.
  • --address 0.0.0.0 exposes it to your whole network.

LOCAL:REMOTEkubectl port-forward svc/orders-db-headless-service 15432:5432 -n jahez-prodpsql to localhost:15432

kubectl run … --rm

Start a throwaway Pod in the namespace and call the Service exactly like an app would.

Creates a Pod, attaches to it, runs the command, deletes the Pod. The call goes through CoreDNS and kube-proxy like real traffic.

💡 Command hint
create a temporary Pod→run the command inside→--rm deletes it

Start a throwaway Pod inside the cluster and run one command there.

kubectlthe Kubernetes CLI; every call talks to the API server of the current context
runcreate a single Pod
curl-check-podobject name
-nnamespace to work in
jahez-prodJahez production namespace
--rmdelete the Pod when the command exits
-itinteractive terminal attached to the Pod
--restart=Nevera bare Pod, not a Deployment; it runs once
--image=curlimages/curl:8.10.1container image of the Pod → curlimages/curl:8.10.1
--everything after this goes to the container, not kubectl
curlmake an HTTP call
-sargument
http://order-api-service/healthURL to call
OUTExample outputexample — needs running Pods
{"status":"Healthy","pod":"order-api-deployment-7d9f8c6b5-m8w4t"}
pod "curl-check-pod" deleted from jahez-prod namespace
✓ Result
Proves DNS, selector, readiness, targetPort and rules in one call.
✕ When it fails
curl: (6) Could not resolve host → DNS/namespace; (7) Failed to connect → no endpoints or wrong targetPort; NetworkPolicy can also block it.

POD requiredtemporary Pod namecurl-check-poddns-check-podkubectl run dns-check-pod -n jahez-prod --rm -it --restart=Never --image=busybox:1.36 -- nslookup order-api-service
--image requiredtool imagebusybox:1.36curlimages/curl:8.10.1nicolaka/netshoot:v0.13kubectl run net-check-pod -n jahez-prod --rm -it --restart=Never --image=nicolaka/netshoot:v0.13 -- dig +short order-api-service.jahez-prod.svc.cluster.local

7.6Troubleshooting

In one sentenceWalk the path in order — exists, valid, has endpoints, endpoints ready, right port, name resolves, nothing blocks — and each real error points at one stage.
#StageWhat you seeCauseCheck
① not foundapply/getError from server (NotFound): services "…" not foundwrong name or namespacekubectl get svc -A | grep order-api
② invalidAPI serverspec.ports[0].name: Required value · provided port is already allocatedfix the field in YAMLkubectl apply -f svc.yaml --dry-run=server
③ no endpointsEndpointSliceEndpoints: <none>selector ≠ Pod labels, or no Podskubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=order-api-service -n jahez-prod
④ not readyreadinessendpoint ready: falsereadinessProbe failingkubectl get pods -l app=order-api -n jahez-prod
⑤ connection refusedtargetPortcurl: (7) Failed to connecttargetPort ≠ port the app listens onkubectl get svc order-api-service -n jahez-prod -o jsonpath='{.spec.ports[*].targetPort}'
⑥ cannot resolveDNSCould not resolve hostother namespace / CoreDNS downkubectl run dns-check-pod -n jahez-prod --rm -it --restart=Never --image=busybox:1.36 -- nslookup order-api-service.jahez-prod
⑦ timeoutNetworkPolicy / rulescurl: (28) timed outpolicy blocks, or kube-proxy stale on a nodekubectl get networkpolicy -n jahez-prod
⑧ <pending>cloud LBEXTERNAL-IP <pending>LB controller missing / wrong class / subnets untaggedkubectl describe svc storefront-gateway-service -n jahez-prod

Checklist, in order

CMDbash
# 1. exists, right namespace?
kubectl get svc order-api-service -n jahez-prod
# 2. anything behind it?
kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=order-api-service -n jahez-prod
# 3. selector vs labels
kubectl get svc order-api-service -n jahez-prod -o jsonpath='{.spec.selector}'
kubectl get pods -n jahez-prod --show-labels | grep order-api
# 4. Pods Ready?
kubectl get pods -l app=order-api -n jahez-prod
# 5. targetPort matches the container?
kubectl get svc order-api-service -n jahez-prod -o jsonpath='{.spec.ports[*].targetPort}'
kubectl get deploy order-api-deployment -n jahez-prod -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].ports}'
# 6. DNS + HTTP from inside
kubectl run curl-check-pod -n jahez-prod --rm -it --restart=Never --image=curlimages/curl:8.10.1 -- curl -sv -m 3 http://order-api-service/health
# 7. policies
kubectl get networkpolicy -n jahez-prod

OUTExample outputexample — needs running Pods

order-api-service-7xk2p   IPv4          8080,9090   10.0.41.23,10.0.77.140,10.0.118.9   0s
Exam traps
  • The container port must actually be named http in the Pod template.
  • During the rollout the slice may hold two slices with different ports — normal.

Lab 4 · NodePort on a fixed port

Task
Expose order-api-deployment on every node at port 30080 via order-api-node-port-service.
What you will build
Show solution
Commands
CMDbash
kubectl expose deploy/order-api-deployment --name=order-api-node-port-service --type=NodePort --port=80 --target-port=8080 -n jahez-prod --dry-run=client -o yaml > np.yaml
# add nodePort: 30080 under ports[0]
kubectl apply -f np.yaml
Full YAML
YAMLorder-api-node-port-service.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: order-api-node-port-service
  namespace: jahez-prod
  labels:
    app: order-api
    purpose: ops-debug
spec:
  # ① Who receives traffic?
  selector:
    app: order-api
  # ② Which ports?
  ports:
    - # ① debug entry on every node
      name: http
      port: 80
      targetPort: http
      nodePort: 30080       # open on every node: <node-ip>:30080
  # ③ Who can reach it?
  type: NodePort
  # ④ How is traffic routed?
  externalTrafficPolicy: Cluster
Verify
CMDbash
kubectl get svc order-api-node-port-service -n jahez-prod
OUTOutputreal output · kube-apiserver v1.34.1
NAME                          TYPE       CLUSTER-IP     EXTERNAL-IP   PORT(S)        AGE
order-api-node-port-service   NodePort       172.20.48.29     <none>                                                 80:30080/TCP      19s
Exam traps
  • 30000-32767 only.
  • Already-used port → provided port is already allocated.

Lab 5 · Headless Service for a StatefulSet

Task
Create orders-db-headless-service so orders-db-stateful-set-0 resolves to its own Pod IP.
What you will build
Show solution
Commands
CMDbash
kubectl create service clusterip orders-db-headless-service --clusterip=None --tcp=5432:5432 -n jahez-prod --dry-run=client -o yaml > hl.yaml
# fix selector to app: orders-db, then
kubectl apply -f hl.yaml
Full YAML
YAMLorders-db-headless-service.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: orders-db-headless-service
  namespace: jahez-prod
  labels:
    app: orders-db
spec:
  # ① Who receives traffic?
  selector:
    app: orders-db
  publishNotReadyAddresses: true   # replicas must find each other before they are Ready
  # ② Which ports?
  ports:
    - # ① PostgreSQL
      name: postgres
      port: 5432
      targetPort: postgres
  # ③ Who can reach it?
  type: ClusterIP
  clusterIP: None                  # headless: no virtual IP, DNS returns Pod IPs
Verify
CMDbash
kubectl run dns-check-pod -n jahez-prod --rm -it --restart=Never --image=busybox:1.36 -- nslookup orders-db-stateful-set-0.orders-db-headless-service
OUTExample outputexample — needs running Pods
Name:	orders-db-stateful-set-0.orders-db-headless-service.jahez-prod.svc.cluster.local
Address: 10.0.41.61
Exam traps
  • serviceName in the StatefulSet must equal the Service name.
  • clusterIP None cannot be added to an existing Service — delete and recreate.

Lab 7 · Debug end to end

Task
menu-api gets "connection refused" from order-api-service. Endpoints exist. Find and fix it.
What you will build
Show solution
Commands
CMDbash
kubectl get svc order-api-service -n jahez-prod -o jsonpath='{.spec.ports[0].targetPort}'
kubectl get deploy order-api-deployment -n jahez-prod -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].ports}'
kubectl patch svc order-api-service -n jahez-prod --type=json -p '[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/ports/0/targetPort","value":8080}]'

CMDbash

OUTExample outputexample — needs running Pods
{"status":"Healthy","pod":"order-api-deployment-7d9f8c6b5-x2kqp"}
Exam traps
  • Endpoints present + connection refused = port problem, not selector.
  • The slice shows the resolved targetPort — compare it with containerPort.

order-api-service.yamlapps/order-api/ · Service · jahez-prod
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: order-api-service
  namespace: jahez-prod
  labels:
    app: order-api
spec:
  # ① Who receives traffic?
  selector:
    app: order-api
  # ② Which ports?
  ports:
    - # ① the API port
      name: http
      protocol: TCP
      appProtocol: http
      port: 80              # callers use order-api-service:80
      targetPort: http      # → containerPort named "http" (8080)
    - # ② the Prometheus port
      name: metrics
      protocol: TCP
      port: 9090
      targetPort: metrics
  # ③ Who can reach it?
  type: ClusterIP           # inside the cluster only
  # ④ How is traffic routed?
  internalTrafficPolicy: Cluster
  trafficDistribution: PreferClose   # prefer Pods in the caller's zone
